content: The relationship between total funding and total blood donations reported across countries reveals significant variations in funding levels per blood collection, particularly when analyzed by income groups. Generally, higher-income countries allocate more funding per blood collection compared to lower-income countries. However, even within the same income group, there are notable differences in funding levels. Alarmingly, many lowand lower-middle-income countries report very low funding per collection or rely heavily on external financial support to sustain their blood services. In terms of funding sources, countries reported varying combinations of government budget allocations, cost recovery mechanisms, and external donor support. For example, some countries rely solely on government budget line items, while others combine government funding with cost recovery or depend entirely on external donors. This reliance on external funding is particularly concerning, as it raises questions about the sustainability of blood services in these regions. The organization of blood collection and processing facilities is critical for efficient and cost-effective resource utilization. National blood services should ideally be coordinated by the Ministry of Health, with activities such as blood screening and processing consolidated in strategic locations. Globally, as of 2013, there were 13,282 blood centers, with 18% operating as stand-alone facilities and 58% based in hospitals. The Western Pacific Region reported the highest proportion of stand-alone blood centers, which also processed the largest number of test samples per screening center compared to other WHO regions. Quality assurance and monitoring systems are essential for ensuring the safety and reliability of blood transfusion services. A total of 155 countries (87% of reporting countries) indicated the existence of national standards for blood collection, testing, processing, storage, and distribution. However, only 55% of countries reported having a system for regular inspection of blood transfusion services, and 57% had a licensing system for these services. Furthermore, 67% of countries reported having a national external quality assessment scheme for laboratory screening of transfusion-transmissible infections, while 52% had similar schemes for blood group serology and compatibility testing. The availability of blood and blood products for transfusion remains a challenge, particularly in low-income countries where blood collection levels are insufficient to meet healthcare system demands. Strategies to improve blood collection, such as promoting regular voluntary non-remunerated blood donation, are critical for ensuring an adequate and sustainable blood supply. Countries with high donor retention rates, such as South Africa, demonstrate lower prevalence rates of transfusion-transmissible infections among donors compared to the general population, highlighting the importance of donor retention strategies. Laboratory screening and testing of donor blood are vital for ensuring blood safety. However, some countries still lack the capacity to test for all markers of transfusion-transmissible infections, compromising the safety of their blood supply. This issue is particularly pronounced in lowand middle-income countries, where the prevalence of such infections among donors is high, but the quality and coverage of blood screening are inadequate. However, many countries lack national guidelines or effective implementation of existing guidelines. Hospital transfusion committees can play a crucial role in optimizing blood use and improving transfusion practices. Policy, legislation, regulatory oversight, and governance mechanisms are fundamental to ensuring the safety, quality, and accessibility of blood and blood products. Governments must integrate adequate and sustainable financing for national blood programs into their healthcare systems. In many lowand lower-middle-income countries, funding for blood services is heavily reliant on external donors, which poses a risk to the sustainability of these services. Transitioning to domestic funding sources is essential for long-term stability. Data collection and reporting systems are critical for managing national blood transfusion programs effectively. Accurate data on blood availability and safety enable countries to prioritize and strengthen their blood systems. Surveillance of infections in blood donors and monitoring transfusion outcomes are necessary to improve safety and reduce risks. Countries should establish standardized systems for data collection and management to enhance donor tracking, traceability, and overall hemovigilance. In conclusion, significant disparities in the availability, safety, and use of blood and blood components persist between developed and developing countries. Blood transfusion safety remains a concern, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, where high rates of transfusion-transmissible infections among donors coincide with inadequate screening and low voluntary blood donation rates.
